newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER SHOWCASE-VALENCIA V BARCELONA FACTS AND FIGURES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-VALENCIA V BARCELONA FACTS AND FIGURES.

text.p: Factfile for the Valencia v Barcelona Spanish league championship game on Sunday
Valencia: Founded in March 1919.

Major honours: League champions (four times) 1942, 1944, 1947, 1971 (won on goal difference from Barcelona). Spanish Cup winners (five times) 1941, 1949, 1954, 1967, 1979. Fairs Cup winners (now UEFA Cup): 1962, 1963. European Cup Winners Cup 1981.

Ground: Mestalla (formerly called Luis Casanova after former president): capacity 49,000. Manager: Jorge Valdano (Argentina) Record appearances: Ricardo Arias (1970s and 80s) 408 games (midfielder Fernando Gomez has 380 games and is still playing). Record goalscorer: Mundo (1940s) 187 goals in 207 games (Argentine World Cup hero Mario Kempes scored 116 goals in 184 games in the 1970s and was twice top goalscorer in the Spanish league).
Barcelona: Founded in 1899 by a Swiss resident in Barcelona, Hans Gamper.

Ground: Camp Nou stadium, (meaning the 'new ground' in the Catalan language), capacity 112,000. Manager: Bobby Robson (England) Record league appearances: Migueli, 391. Record league goalscorer: Cesar Rodriguez, 174

Encounters between the two sides: (Valencia first) In Valencia: played 61, won 25, drawn 14, lost 22 In Barcelona: played 62, won 7, drawn 17, lost 38. Last five corresponding fixtures (1991-92 first): 3-1, 3-4, 0-4, 1-2, 4-1 Last season (March 9 1996) Valencia 4 (Fernando Gomez, Viola, Mijatovic 2) Barcelona 1 (Guillermo Amor)
Barcelona were the first Spanish league champions in 1929 and share with Real Madrid and Athletic Bilbao the honour of never having been relegated from the first division.
Valencia spent three of the league's early years in the second division and were relegated in the 1985-86 season. They were promoted again at the first try.

Barcelona boast the largest number of season-ticket holders of any club in Europe -- 108,000 -- and averaged gates of 81,000 last season. Valencia managed an average 43,000 in a season in which they finished second.

Barcelona's Camp Nou held the final of the 1992 Olympic tournament -- in which Spain beat Poland -- and the opening ceremony of the 1982 World Cup. Valencia has held several important Spanish World Cup qualifying games in recent years after the decision to take the monopoly on these games away from Seville.

Valencia have tried to change their image in recent years by turning back the clock in some areas. The players now wear the white shirts, black shorts and socks that the team first wore at its foundation in 1919 after a period in which the strip was all white.

The Valencia ground, which was severely damaged by rain storms in the late 1950s, had been named after the club president who did most to rescue the club from the setback -- Luis Casanova. However club officials have tried to get back to their roots by renaming it 'Mestalla' after the area it stands in.

With the wealth of foreign stars now arriving in the first side, many younger players move on from Barcelona reserve sides to other teams. More than 20 such players are currently active in the Spanish first and second divisions.
Barcelona reserves play in the Mini estadi, a 16,500-seat stadium adjoining the Camp Nou that is considerably bigger than several first division grounds.
Barcelona games always begin with the singing of the club hymn in the local Catalan language.
Barcelona are universally known as Barca.

Valencia have Spanish football's most famous fan -- Manolo. The robust Manolo, who always wears an outsize beret, accompanies the Spanish team by banging a huge drum and is enormously popular with supporters. He owns a bar, which he calls the 'museum' because of the quantity of footballing paraphernalia in it, next to Valencia's Mestalla ground.

Barcelona's claret and blue colours are incorporated into the club shield alongside the red and yellow stripes of the Catalan flag and the red cross of Sant Jordi, which appears in England as the cross of Saint George.

Jordi, the patron saint of Catalonia, is a favourite name for local boys. Former Barcelona player, and later coach, Johan Cruyff followed tradition by naming his son -- now a striker at Manchester United -- after the saint.

Valencia's shield incorporates a bat, a symbol of the city after its reconquest by the Christian King Jaime in the 13th century. Jaime and his men are said to have spent the night before the decisive attack sheltering in a cave.

Brazilian striker Leandro paid homage to the club by celebrating his goals with a bat imitation. He subsequently adopted the position of a dog cocking its leg but has abandoned that because of complaints from other players and says he will change his routine to another animal.

The Barcelona organisation also includes teams in several other sports. Barcelona's basketball and handball teams are amongst the most successful in Europe and there are also roller-hockey, hockey, ice-hockey, athletics, rugby, baseball, indoor soccer, volleyball and skating sides.
